chapter: The 1940s: small groups, Teddy Wilson and Ethel Waters
title: With James P. Johnson at Cafe Society
summary: Thomas worked with James P. Johnson's small group around 1940. One night Johnson played the St. Louis Blues in a way that silenced the room.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: I told him I didn't like uniforms ... so in the '40s I started to work for James P. Johnson.
I think it might have come by through Fats Waller at Cafe Society.
Maurice Johnson and Gene, trombonist, Big Joe Watts, George Charlie Johnson, Gene Simon, yeah. Back in around 1940.
Gene Simon was the tenor player?
No, he played trombone. He worked for the Redman band sometime before. Do you remember Gene Simon?
Yeah. And, then, let's see, with Joe Sullivan.

James P. Did you know, you know his work. He's a tremendous person. And, since we're talking about it, I've heard a lot of things happen, you know, and he's a tremendous musician and I've heard lot of things happen with the piano and different instruments. So, one night I think John was in there, John Hammond was in there that particular night and he made a request. Now, James' approach to music was wonderful. We never played the "Charleston", we never played "Ivy Cling to Me". We never played those things. We had a song called, came out called "You, You, You", the show he started called The Gamblers. "Yamekraw" was one of his things.

Yeah. Well, what he did one night ... Stan, and Babe, he you played the "St. Louis Blues", that should have been in the never played a thing like that. Handy should have heard that (card)... It was a silence that happens to few people. And, after that, it's something else. Yeah, I think that was '40.
